procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 02.12.2016 of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M-No. 27311 of 2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner applied for bail before the Additional Sessions Judge, Rohtak which was dismissed on 12th July, 2016. Though some of the co-accused were granted bail by the High Court, bail application of the petitioner was dismissed by the High Court on 2nd December, 2016. The High Court observed that prima facie the petitioner appeared to be the leader of the mob which indulged in arson, loot and mischief of burning of the house of a Cabinet Minister.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner approached the Supreme Court after the High Court declined bail. The Supreme Court did not grant bail but directed that the trial be concluded as far as possible within six months. Later, CBI filed an application (M.A. No. 267 of 2017 in SLP (Crl.) No. 657 of 2017) in the disposed of matter for modification of the Supreme Court's order dated 31st January, 2017. The Supreme Court put up the matter for further consideration on 3rd July, 2018.

directions: CBI must complete investigation at the most within next two months so that trial can commence latest by July 10, 2018 and concluded by the end of the year.
It will be open to the petitioner, if he is still in custody, to move a bail application before the trial court in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether a timeline should be set for the completion of the CBI investigation and the subsequent trial, considering the prolonged custody of the accused.

facts: The accused had been in custody for more than two years.
The investigation was transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), which had been investigating the case for over one and a half years.
The CBI had not provided any clear indication of the progress made in the investigation or a justification for why more time was required.
law: The Supreme Court recognized that a speedy investigation is a fundamental right, part of the right to a fair procedure under Article 21 of the Constitution.
No investigating agency is permitted to take an unduly long time to complete an investigation.

While there is no express outer time limit for completing investigations in all cases (unlike provisions for default bail under Section 167 Cr.P.C.), an inordinate delay, especially when the accused is in custody, can make the procedure unreasonable and is not conducive to the administration of criminal justice.
application: The Court applied the principles of Article 21 to the specific facts of the case.
It found that the period of over one and a half years taken by the CBI for investigation, coupled with the accused's custody of over two years, constituted an undue delay.

The Court reasoned that this prolonged period without the commencement of a trial, and without sufficient justification from the CBI, was a violation of the accused's fundamental right to a speedy investigation and trial.
reasoning.conclusion: Considering the prolonged custody of the accused and the undue delay in the investigation, the Supreme Court accepted the need for a timeline. It directed the CBI to complete its investigation within the next two months, so that the trial could commence by July 10, 2018, and be concluded by the end of that year.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner should be granted the liberty to move a fresh bail application before the trial court, given that the previous bail order was passed over a year ago.

facts: The petitioner had been in custody for more than two years.
The investigation by the CBI had been pending for over one and a half years.
The previous order from the Supreme Court declining bail was passed on January 30, 2017, which was more than a year before the current hearing.
law: The Court implicitly recognizes that a significant passage of time and delay in investigation can constitute a change in circumstances, justifying a fresh consideration for bail.
The Court noted that speedy investigation is a recognized part of the fundamental right to a fair procedure under Article 21 of the Constitution.
application: The Court observed that a significant amount of time—over one year—had passed since its last order declining bail.
During this period, the petitioner remained in custody while the investigation was still pending and the trial had not commenced.
reasoning.conclusion: Based on the fact that more than a year had gone by since the last bail order was passed, the Supreme Court granted the petitioner the liberty to move a fresh bail application before the trial court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A delay in investigation may affect the reasonableness of the procedure, especially when a person is in custody and unable to furnish bail, thereby necessitating the establishment of timelines for completing investigations to give effect to the mandate of Article 21 of the Constitution.
obiter: A Magistrate cannot authorise detention in police custody beyond 15 days.
After judicial custody for more than 90 days in serious cases and 60 days in other cases, there is a provision for mandatory default bail if the investigation is delayed beyond the said period.
In a summons case, if the investigation is not concluded within six months, it must be stopped unless its continuation is found necessary.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The constitutional mandate for a speedy trial under Article 21 implicitly includes the right to a speedy investigation. While it is not feasible to prescribe a mandatory outer time limit for all investigations, inordinate delay, particularly when the accused is in custody, may be taken as presumptive proof of prejudice. In such cases, the court must intervene to balance the relevant factors and prevent the prosecution from becoming a form of persecution by setting timelines to ensure the investigation is completed without undue delay.
legal_tests_applied: To determine whether an undue delay has occurred, the court must have regard to the nature of the offence, the number of accused and witnesses, the workload of the court and the investigating agency, and systemic delays. This is a balancing test to weigh the relevant factors in each individual case on the anvil of Article 21 of the Constitution.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's (CBI) argument that the investigation was a voluminous and time-consuming task was insufficient to justify an indefinite delay. The court subordinated this practical difficulty to the respondent's fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21, which encompasses a speedy investigation.

The court held that prolonged custody during an investigation creates a presumption of prejudice against the accused. The appellant's justification for delay did not overcome this presumption, leading the court to conclude that intervention was necessary to prevent the prosecution from becoming persecution.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was vindicated because the court affirmed that the right to a speedy trial under Article 21 is a fundamental right that extends to the investigation phase, as established in precedents like Hussainara Khatoon and Abdul Rehman Antulay.

The court's reasoning that "Inordinate delay may be taken as presumptive proof of prejudice particularly when accused is in custody so that prosecution does not become persecution" directly supported the respondent's implied claim that their prolonged incarceration necessitated judicial intervention to set a timeline for the investigation and trial.
policy_considerations: The court articulated a core policy that the justice system must ensure that "prosecution does not become persecution" through inordinate delays, especially when an individual's liberty is curtailed by custody.

Recognizing a systemic problem beyond the individual case, the court noted "there is certainly a need for in-house mechanism to ensure that there is no undue delay in completing investigation." This led to a broader directive for the Ministry of Home Affairs to engage with all investigating agencies to address systemic delays, reflecting a concern for procedural fairness across the entire criminal justice system.
